![A screenshot from the article showing a public GitHub catalog of "Act as…" prompt-injection examples — the kind of hit that dominates Common Crawl false positives. Image from [Google Online Security Blog](https://security.googleblog.com/2026/04/ai-threats-in-wild-current-state-of.html).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

Thomas Brunner, Yu-Han Liu, and Moni Pande on the [Google Online Security Blog](https://security.googleblog.com/2026/04/ai-threats-in-wild-current-state-of.html) ran a sweep of Common Crawl for indirect prompt injection (IPI) patterns and report what they actually found across billions of pages of the public English-speaking web:

- The dominant signal is false positives. Most "prompt injection" text on the public web is research papers, educational blog posts, and security articles discussing the topic.
- Confirmed in-the-wild categories:
    - **Harmless pranks** — invisible injections that change a chatbot's conversational tone.
    - **Helpful guidance** — instructions asking AI summaries to add useful context for the reader.
    - **SEO** — instructions that try to manipulate AI assistants into promoting a business over its competitors, including elaborate auto-generated payloads.
    - **Deterring AI agents** — variations on "if you are an AI, do not crawl this site," including one that lures AI readers onto a page that streams an infinite, never-finishing response.
    - **Malicious: exfiltration** — small number, low sophistication, mostly individual experiments. No sign of advanced exfiltration prompts published by security researchers in 2025 being deployed at scale.
    - **Malicious: destruction** — instructions to delete files on the user's machine. "Potentially devastating" but unlikely to succeed as written.
- A 32% relative increase in malicious detections between November 2025 and February 2026, measured across multiple Common Crawl snapshots.
